title: Cross-border mergers and acquisitions and the role of trade costs
abstract: Cross-border mergers and acquisitions (M&As) have increased dramatically over the last two decades. This paper analyses the role of trade costs in explaining the increase in the number of cross-border M&As. In particular, we distinguish horizontal and non-horizontal M&As and investigate whether trade costs affect these two types of mergers differently. We analyse this question using industry data for 23 OECD countries for the period 1990-2001. Our findings suggest that while in the aggregate trade costs affect cross-border merger activity negatively its impact differs importantly across horizontal and non-horizontal mergers. The impact of trade costs is less negative for horizontal mergers, which is consistent with the tariff-jumping argument.
summary_en: Cross-border mergers and acquisitions (M&As) surged in the 1990s and 2000s. Hijzen, Görg and Manchin test whether trade costs help explain this. Using industry data for 23 OECD countries 1990-2001, they distinguish horizontal mergers (same industry, often tariff-jumping motivated) from non-horizontal mergers (vertical or conglomerate). They find that on average, lower trade costs spur more cross-border M&A — but the relationship differs sharply by type. Horizontal mergers respond less negatively to trade costs, consistent with the tariff-jumping motive: when tariffs fall, firms substitute exports for affiliates.
data_used: Industry-level cross-border M&A data for 23 OECD countries 1990-2001 from Thomson Financial Securities Data Company (SDC), combined with bilateral tariff data and other trade-cost measures.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian inward-FDI policy. The paper shows that tariff reductions through EU integration drove some M&A inflows in the 1990s but that horizontal M&As (tariff-jumping) are less sensitive — a Hungarian-relevant pattern given the high share of foreign-owned manufacturing. Useful for HIPA and Pénzügyminisztérium when analysing how EU trade integration interacts with FDI.
